(a) 
In General.—The following laws of the District of Columbia (as in effect on the date of the enactment of this Act) shall apply to the members and activities of the Authority:

        (1) 
Section 742 of the District of Columbia Self-Government and Governmental Reorganization Act (sec. 1–1504, D.C. Code).
 
        (2) 
Sections 201 through 206 of the District of Columbia Freedom of Information Act (secs. 1–1521 through 1–1526, D.C. Code).
 
        (3) 
Section 601 of the District of Columbia Campaign Finance Reform and Conflict of Interest Act (sec. 1–1461, D.C. Code).
  
    (b) 
No Control, Supervision, Oversight, or Review by Mayor or Council.—

        (1) 
In general.—Neither the Mayor nor the Council may exercise any control, supervision, oversight, or review over the Authority or its activities.
 
        (2) 
Prohibition against legislation affecting authority.—Section 602(a) of the District of Columbia Self-Government and Governmental Reorganization Act (sec. 1–233(a), D.C.  Code) is amended—

            (A) 
by striking “or” at the end of paragraph (8);
 
            (B) 
by striking the period at the end of paragraph (9) and inserting “; or”; and
 
            (C) 
by adding at the end the following new paragraph:


“(10) 
enact any act, resolution, or rule with respect to the District of Columbia Financial Responsibility and Management Assistance Authority established under section 101(a) of the District of Columbia Financial Responsibility and Management Assistance Act of 1995.”.



   
    (c) 
Authority Not Subject to Representation by Corporation Counsel.—In any action brought by or on behalf of the Authority, and in any action brought against the Authority, the Authority shall be represented by such counsel as it may select, but in no instance may the Authority be represented by the Corporation Counsel of the District of Columbia.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that applying D.C. open-meetings and freedom-of-information laws to the Authority, and mentioning actions "brought against the Authority", amounts to public participation or a right to sue. But these are bare cross-references to transparency and ethics laws plus a rule about which counsel represents the Authority; none of it requires consultation, comment, hearings, or grants a right to challenge a decision. The section in fact bars the Mayor and Council (local government) from any oversight or review of the Authority, which is the opposite of involving outside parties.
fable.s: Neither the Mayor nor the Council may exercise any control, supervision, oversight, or review over the Authority or its activities.

opus.w: The section applies certain D.C. laws to the Authority by citation, bars the Mayor and Council from controlling it, and sets out who represents it in court. Nothing in the text sets up a comment period, a hearing, consultation or an outside advisory role before a federal decision. The reference to actions 'brought against the Authority' is about legal representation, not a grant of a right to sue. A cited D.C. law may require open meetings, but the text itself doesn't say so, and the Authority is a D.C. entity, so the 'Yes' reading is weak.
opus.s: The following laws of the District of Columbia (as in effect on the date of the enactment of this Act) shall apply to the members and activities of the Authority
opus.b:
1. **Tempting but wrong reading.** Section 742 of the D.C. Home Rule Act is, I believe, the District's open-meetings rule, and it is applied here along with D.C.'s Freedom of Information Act. That could look like a "public meeting before a decision." The section also mentions lawsuits "brought against the Authority," which could look like a right to sue.

2. **Why that reading fails.** The section never actually says there must be a public meeting, comment period, consultation or advisory body. It only applies D.C. ethics, records and conduct laws to the Authority by citing section numbers. The Authority is also set up as an entity inside the D.C. government, so this is not clearly a federal decision-maker bringing in outsiders. Subsection (b) cuts the Mayor and Council *out* of any oversight role. Subsection (c) only says who represents the Authority in court; it does not give anyone a right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: This section primarily establishes that the District of Columbia Mayor and Council are prohibited from exercising control or oversight over the Authority. While it incorporates the DC Freedom of Information Act, FOIA is a transparency tool for accessing records after the fact, not a mechanism for consultation or coordination before a decision is made. The text does not require the federal government to consult with outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) in making decisions; rather, it limits the role of local government officials.
qwen_chat.s: Neither the Mayor nor the Council may exercise any control, supervision, oversight, or review over the Authority or its activities.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that applying the District of Columbia Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) implies public participation because it allows the public to access government records. However, the definition of participation requires consultation, coordination, or decision-making involvement *before* a federal decision is made. FOIA is a post-hoc transparency mechanism, not a participatory process in the decision-making itself. Furthermore, the section primarily focuses on insulating the Authority from local government oversight (Mayor/Council), which is an exclusion of participation rather than a requirement for it. The actors involved in the restrictions (Mayor, Council, Corporation Counsel) are local government officials, but the text does not mandate their input; it explicitly prohibits their control.
